summary: Specifies how the SDP offer/answer exchange can be used to set up a WebRTC data channel out of band, instead of using the in-band Data Channel Establishment Protocol. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: There are two ways to agree on a message lane between two programs: talk about it while using it, or arrange it beforehand. This document explains the arranged-beforehand way, using the call setup messages.

questions: how to negotiate data channels in sdp
what is out-of-band data channel negotiation
dcep vs sdp data channel negotiation
subtitle: Opening WebRTC data channels with the SDP offer/answer exchange instead of in-band messages.

tldr.problem: Data channels can be set up in-band with the Data Channel Establishment Protocol (DCEP), but DCEP negotiates only transport parameters, not parameters of the protocol carried on the channel.
tldr.mechanism: Two media-level SDP attributes are defined. a=dcmap: describes each data channel (stream id, label, subprotocol, ordering, reliability, priority), and a=dcsa: carries subprotocol attributes for it. Both go through normal offer/answer.
tldr.outcome: Applications can negotiate channels and their subprotocol settings in the same signaling used for the rest of the session, and data may be sent only once the peer has the channel set up.

today: RFC 8864 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. Its metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Out-of-Band Data Channel Setup
sections.content:
A WebRTC data channel is a bidirectional channel made of paired SCTP streams that share one stream identifier. The data channel protocol is described in RFC 8831, and the in-band Data Channel Establishment Protocol (DCEP) is in RFC 8832. Other in-band or out-of-band protocols may also be used to set channels up.

This RFC defines SDP offer/answer procedures, building on RFC 3264, for negotiating data channels out of band, meaning through the application signaling path instead of through the SCTP association. They rest on the generic rules for SCTP over DTLS in RFC 8841.

The mechanism applies only to SDP used with offer/answer. Declarative SDP is out of scope and undefined. MSRP and BFCP appear in examples only to illustrate the generic procedures, and the document does not fully specify how to run MSRP over a data channel.
sections.plainLanguage: You can agree on a secret tunnel by whispering through it, or by writing a note beforehand. This document is about the note.

sections.title: The a=dcmap Attribute
sections.content:
a=dcmap: is a media-level attribute that defines the parameters of one data channel. It begins with the stream id (one to five digits), the SCTP stream identifier that forms the channel. Optional parameters follow, separated by semicolons:

  • label: the channel name, which defaults to the empty string.
  • subprotocol: the protocol expected on the channel, which defaults to the empty string.
  • ordered: true or false, with true as default.
  • max-retr or max-time: partial reliability by number of retransmissions or by lifetime in milliseconds. Both MUST NOT be present together. With neither, delivery is reliable.
  • priority: the channel priority relative to other channels on the association, with 256 assumed when absent.

These parameters map to the fields of the DCEP open message in RFC 8832. The attribute creates a bidirectional channel, and its values are fixed properties rather than something the answerer renegotiates. Quoted strings such as labels are written as UTF-8 bytes, with bytes that cannot appear directly written as % followed by two hex digits.
sections.plainLanguage: The line is a name tag and a rule sheet for one lane: its number, its name, whether messages must arrive in order, and how hard to try again if one is lost.

sections.title: The a=dcsa Attribute
sections.content:
A subprotocol often needs its own SDP attributes. For example, MSRP would normally use a=accept-types. On a data channel, each such attribute is wrapped as a=dcsa:stream-id original-attribute, where dcsa stands for data channel subprotocol attribute and the stream id ties the line to the matching a=dcmap:. So a=accept-types:text/plain becomes a=dcsa:2 accept-types:text/plain.

Unlike dcmap parameters, dcsa attributes are negotiated by offer/answer following the rules of the subprotocol's own documents. Attributes that do not depend on the transport are used as in the original specification. If a subprotocol has offer/answer rules elsewhere but none for dcsa, implementations SHOULD assume the default values of all negotiable parameters. Not every SDP attribute suits dcsa.

Both attributes have multiplexing category SPECIAL. No multiplexing rules are given because several SCTP associations over one DTLS association are outside the scope of RFC 8841.
sections.plainLanguage: Some lanes carry special games with their own rules. Each rule is written on a card tagged with the lane number so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Procedures
sections.content:
One media description can describe several data channels, each with its own a=dcmap: line, and they can be created, changed and closed in different exchanges. To avoid stream id collisions, the endpoint acting as DTLS client MUST use even identifiers and the DTLS server MUST use odd ones. Ids of channels negotiated with DCEP MUST NOT appear in SDP.

The offerer SHALL add an a=dcmap: line for the channel in the media section for the SCTP association, and MAY add a=dcsa: lines with a matching stream id. An answerer that accepts the channel SHALL include the dcmap line, with the stream id, max-retr and max-time values identical to the offer, and MAY add dcsa lines. A message with both max-retr and max-time must be rejected by the receiver of an offer, and an answer with both makes the exchange fail.

If the answer lacks a channel's dcmap line, the offerer SHALL close that channel. The DTLS and SCTP associations are still set up, and DCEP can then be used. Each application MUST wait to send data until the channel is confirmed at the peer, which for the offerer is when the answer confirms it or data from the peer begins to arrive, whichever comes first.

To close a channel, an endpoint sends an SCTP SSN Reset and then a new offer that removes the channel's dcmap and dcsa lines, or reuses the stream with a different dcmap value. A dcsa line with no dcmap line is an error and is discarded, and an unknown dcsa attribute SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: One kid offers a lane with rules, and the other either agrees to the exact same rules or says no. Nobody may use the lane until both are sure it exists.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples with an m=application line using UDP/DTLS/SCTP webrtc-datachannel. In the first, the offer carries a BFCP channel with stream id 0 and the answer has no dcmap line, so the offerer closes that channel. The SCTP association is still set up over DTLS, and either side may then use DCEP.

In the second, the offer has a BFCP channel (stream id 0) and an MSRP channel (stream id 2) with dcsa lines. The answer accepts MSRP and drops BFCP, which leaves stream id 0 free for later use. In the third, the offerer removes the MSRP channel with stream id 2 and opens a new MSRP channel with stream id 4, and the answerer accepts the whole offer.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a lane being refused, a lane being half-accepted, and an old lane being swapped for a new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new attributes are negotiated while opening an SCTP channel over DTLS as specified in RFC 8841. This RFC adds no security considerations beyond that one. Each subprotocol may have its own, to be documented in its definition.

Error cases, such as unknown parameter values or breaking the odd/even stream id rule, MUST be handled by closing the data channel concerned.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes travel through the same locked tunnel as everything else, so no new locks are needed. If a note breaks the rules, that lane is closed.
